implementation_notes: asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) is the event-loop load leveller: await put() suspends while the queue holds N items and await get() suspends while it is empty, so the bound paces producers without blocking the loop; the queue is explicitly not thread-safe and belongs to one loop. Workers are tasks, task_done()/join() track completion, and since 3.13 shutdown() unblocks waiters cleanly at shutdown. The classic threads-plus-queue structure is replaced by one queue and a handful of tasks; threads are only needed for blocking libraries, which must then run in an executor.
code_sketch:
queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1000)          # await put() suspends when full
async def worker():
    while True:
        job = await queue.get()              # waits while empty
        try:
            await process(job)
        finally:
            queue.task_done()
workers = [asyncio.create_task(worker()) for _ in range(8)]
await queue.put(job)                         # paced, never dropped
pitfalls: asyncio.Queue(maxsize=0) is unbounded - the default - and silently removes the bound.
A blocking call inside a worker (requests, time.sleep, sync DB driver) stalls the whole loop, so the queue stops draining; offload with loop.run_in_executor or asyncio.to_thread.
Forgetting task_done() leaves queue.join() blocked forever, which hangs graceful shutdown.
put_nowait() raising QueueFull is the explicit shed path; catching it and dropping silently loses work without a trace.

variants.name: queue.Queue(maxsize) with worker threads
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library's queue module implements multi-producer, multi-consumer queues with all the locking included: Queue(maxsize=N) blocks put() once the queue is full and get() while it is empty, put_nowait() raises Full as the shed path, and task_done()/join() report when the work is actually processed. Threads are the right consumer here when the processing is synchronous or I/O-bound via blocking libraries; because of the GIL they do not deliver CPU parallelism, so CPU-bound stages need processes (multiprocessing.Queue) or a broker. The classic hand-written lock-and-condition-variable queue is exactly what this class already is.
variants.code_sketch:
q = queue.Queue(maxsize=1000)                  # insertion blocks once full
def worker():
    while True:
        job = q.get()                            # blocks while empty
        try:
            process(job)
        finally:
            q.task_done()
threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True).start()
q.put(job)                                       # paced, not dropped
q.join()
pitfalls: ThreadPoolExecutor.submit() queues without limit, so max_workers bounds threads but not the backlog; a bounded queue must sit in front.
Daemon workers die silently at exit, possibly mid-item; shutdown needs a sentinel plus join().
The GIL means threads bound memory and latency but not CPU: queue a process pool or a broker for CPU-bound work.
maxsize<=0 (the constructor default) is unbounded - the failure mode the pattern prevents.

variants.name: Celery workers over a broker (Redis/RabbitMQ)
variants.implementation_notes: When the queue must outlive the process or feed several machines, Celery moves the buffer to a broker: task.delay() enqueues into Redis/RabbitMQ and worker processes drain it, with --concurrency setting the workers per node, prefetch controlling how much each worker reserves, acks_late deciding when a task is acknowledged, and the worker shutting down warm or cold on TERM/QUIT. The pattern's leveling is now the broker backlog and the consumer count, and retries plus the reserved/failed sets cover the retry and dead-letter parts. In-process asyncio or threading queues remain the lighter choice when durability is not required.
pitfalls: Prefetch multiplies the effective queue: a worker reserves several tasks ahead, so work sits unprocessed while the backlog looks healthy.
acks_late (needed for crash safety) makes redelivery common, so tasks must be idempotent.
Broker persistence and visibility-timeout settings decide whether accepted work survives a restart or a long task.
Blocking Celery calls inside an asyncio service need run_in_executor or the loop stalls.
